content: Coffea, commonly known as coffee, is a genus that includes ten species of flowering plants belonging to the Rubiaceae family. These plants are either shrubs or small trees and are indigenous to subtropical regions of Africa and southern Asia. The seeds of these plants, referred to as coffee beans in trade, are the primary source of the popular stimulating beverage known as coffee. Coffee beans are extensively cultivated in tropical countries, where they are grown on plantations for both local consumption and export to temperate regions. Coffee is one of the most significant global commodity crops and serves as a major export product for several countries. The coffee plant can grow up to 5 meters (10–12 feet) in height and is capable of enduring severe pruning. However, it cannot thrive in areas where winter frost occurs. Optimal growth is achieved at high elevations, and to maximize the yield of coffee berries (800–1400 kg per hectare), the plants require substantial amounts of water and fertilizer. In some cases, calcium carbonate and other lime minerals are applied to reduce soil acidity, which can result from mineral runoff in mountainous areas. The caffeine content in coffee beans acts as a natural defense mechanism, deterring many organisms from consuming the seeds, similar to how nicotine functions in tobacco leaves. While several Coffea species can be cultivated for their beans, Coffea arabica is widely regarded as producing the highest quality coffee. Other species, such as Coffea canephora (var. robusta), are typically grown in areas unsuitable for Coffea arabica. The coffee tree produces red or purple fruits, known as drupes or coffee berries, each containing two seeds, which are the coffee beans. In approximately 5–10% of any coffee crop, a cherry will contain only a single bean instead of the usual two. This is referred to as a peaberry, which has a distinct flavor profile with a higher concentration of flavors, particularly acidity, due to its smaller size. Peaberries are often separated from the main yield and either sold as a specialty product (e.g., New Guinea Peaberry) or discarded. The coffee tree begins to bear fruit after 3–5 years and continues to do so for approximately 50–60 years, though some trees can live up to 100 years. The blossoms of the coffee tree resemble jasmine in both color and fragrance. The fruit takes about nine months to ripen. Globally, an estimated 15 billion coffee trees are cultivated on approximately 100,000 square kilometers of land. Coffee also serves as a food source for the larvae of certain Lepidoptera species, including Dalceridae, the Turnip Moth, and some members of the genus Endoclita, such as E. damor and E. malabaricus. After harvesting, coffee beans undergo a series of processing steps. The beans are first pulped, usually with a mechanical pulper, to remove most of the soft flesh. They are then fermented, often through wet fermentation in water for 10 to 36 hours, to eliminate the remaining sticky mucilage. Following fermentation, the beans are washed and dried, typically under the sun. This process is labor-intensive, time-consuming, and costly for most growers. At this stage, the beans are referred to as milled beans. Once the raw (or green) coffee beans reach their destination country, they are roasted. Roasting darkens the beans' color, alters their internal chemistry, and enhances their flavor and aroma. Blending may occur either before or after roasting to ensure a consistent flavor profile. However, roasted beans are highly perishable. It is estimated that 10 million people are employed on coffee plantations in the countries where coffee is grown. A single worker can harvest 50–100 kilograms of coffee fruits per day, yielding 10–20 kilograms of raw coffee. Brazil and Colombia account for 40% of global coffee production, with Brazil contributing 30% and Colombia 10%. As of 1998, global coffee production was approximately 100 million sacks. Many farmers receive low prices for their coffee due to a global market slump, which has led to the availability of fair trade coffee in many countries. In its natural environment, Coffea plants grow under shade. However, most commercial coffee is produced on full-sun plantations, some of which were established through deforestation. Shade-grown coffee naturally mulches its surroundings, has a longer lifespan (twice as long as sun-grown varieties), and depletes fewer soil resources. Shade-grown coffee is also believed by some to be of higher quality, as the smaller cherries produced under shade concentrate the flavors into the seed (bean). Additionally, shade-grown coffee is associated with environmentally friendly ecosystems that support a greater variety and number of migratory birds compared to sun-grown coffee farms.
